read_for: In 1881 the Gaddis spend the winter in Kangra and the summer across the range in Chamba.
In 1961 the flocks go to Kangra, Nurpur and Pathankot in October and November.
Barnes places cultivation between 3,500 and 7,000 feet, with little above that height.
The passes are closed by snow from the middle of November until May.
The Kugti pass is over 16,000 feet high, and a crossing takes three days on the tops. Lower down, the pasture lies among forests.
Newell describes the Gaddi country as a series of river sections of about 40 miles each.
Brahmaur lies on the Budhal stream, which joins the Ravi.
The villagers buy timber from the Brahmni reserved forest at reduced rates through the Forest Department.
Forests occupy the largest area of the village. The villagers take firewood, timber and grass from them.
The livestock table lists the sheep and goats of each caste in a high village. The figures were read from the page image.
Shakrori stands at 1,700 feet.
Tandi stands at ten thousand feet.
Chaupal stands at 7,685 feet on the Yamuna side and keeps few sheep and goats.
In 1881 the Gaddis spend half the year, the winter months, in the valleys of Kangra.
In 1881 Barnes describes the hill Gujars moving to the summer grass. Rose later copies this passage.
In 1911 the flocks leave for Kangra in October and November and return in April and May.
Rose's account of the Gujars copies the 1881 census, page 267, so the two pages count as one witness.
In 1931 the hill people of the high ranges spend the winter in the valleys and plains.
In 1961, 61 of Brahmaur's 99 households move out in winter.
In 1961 the Gaddis stay in Pangi from July to September. The attempt of 1874 to lease the high pastures is described on the same page.
The Gujjars go up in May and return in September. The Gaddis of Maingal are settled farmers.
The Kinnaur flocks spend the winter in Bilaspur, Arki, Mehlog, Karsog, Seoni and Sirmur until the end of April.
The wife usually goes with her husband on the winter route.
Women carry an equal load during the migration.
Map 252 is a map of the sheep in each tahsil of Punjab, including Kangra, Kulu, Lahaul and Spiti, and Simla.
Map 253 is a map of the goats in each tahsil.
The notes to maps 252 and 253 state that sheep "are more numerous in the hilly Districts of Kangra, Simla and parts of Lahaul & Spiti" and "live mainly on grazing".
Kanum lies two miles above the Sutlej.
The people of Kanum go down in winter with flocks loaded with chilgozas, wool and herbs, and sell them at the Lavi fair.
In Bir, 24 households own 139 goats and 69 sheep. The animals were bought from Gaddis in winter for 10 to 12 rupees.
The people of Batal buy wool from the Kinnauras who stay near the village in winter.
Shakrori's animals were bought from passing Kinnauras. The moneylender, a shopkeeper at Seoni, is described on the same page.
A malundi tends his own flock. Hired shepherds, called pohals, are employed only in rare cases. Their wage is listed on the same page.
Farmers send their sheep and goats up with paid graziers, at 20 to 25 naye paise per animal for the season.
Grazing permits are valid from 1 June to 15 October. Devi-Kothi's flocks per household are listed on the same page.
Newell states that most Gaddis are not shepherds.
The Gaddis sell woollen gardus in the low hills during their winter stay.
From Tibet the traders bring wool, pasham, butter, ghee, sheep and salt, and exchange them for rice, cloth and utensils.
A trader leaves for Tibet in July and returns by November. He pays four hired shepherds, called fawals, Rs 60 a year each.
The Lavi fair is held at Rampur in the second week of November.
Rose records Tibetan trade sheep crossing the Baralacha pass.
The ruler of Bushahr is the Primary Owner of the land. The villagers owe him revenue and a labour service called Athada Begar.
Every villager has a right to use the pastures. A jeepable road has been built to the village.
In Chamba all grazing rights belonged to the raja, in contrast with the common pastures of Kanum.
Brahmans and Rajputs are 83 of 99 households. Forty of these households own flocks, and they hold 4,391 of the 4,484 sheep and goats. The figures were read from the page image.
Rajputs hold 2,416 of 2,557 sheep and goats, and Kolis, Lohars and Badhis hold few. The figures were read from the page image.
Kanets hold 1,744 sheep and goats and Kolis hold 83. The figures were read from the page image.
Bodhs hold 336 of 363 sheep. The figures were read from the page image.
In the Pangi villages, Rajputs and Brahmins hold 554 of 596 sheep and goats. The figures were read from the page image.
A family keeps 100 to 200 sheep and goats on average, and the Lambardar keeps about 1,100. Households with large flocks send one or two members as shepherds.
In Rajana, Kolis hold 302 of 488 goats, which is an exception to the pattern. The figures were read from the page image.
Hired shepherds, called fawals, receive Rs 60 a year with meals and 8 kg of wool.
From May to September, every household pays the village shepherd one patha of buckwheat per sheep or goat.
Gujjars owe debts in food grain to Gaddi Brahmins.
The debt table is arranged by income group. Every Gujjar household is in debt, at 30 per cent interest.
The Gujjars sell their ghee to one shopkeeper at Chamba below the market price.
Gujjars in debt are obliged to sell their produce to the shopkeepers who lend to them.
The landlord is also the moneylender to the Scheduled Castes.
The debt table is arranged by income group. Lenders charge interest of five seers per maund on loans of grain.
The debt table is arranged by cause. Twelve of 36 households are in debt.
The debt table is arranged by income group. The prices charged by the shopkeeper from Kangra are described on the same page.
Tenants pay their interest in agricultural labour.
The Gaddis hold land in both Kangra and Chamba. When fined in Kangra, they paid the same fine into the Chamba treasury.
Gaddis crossing into Lahul paid grazing tax to both the Chamba ruler and the Lahul ruler.
The raja could dispose only of the right to use the land.
All grazing rights belonged to the raja. He auctioned the right to collect grazing fees, usually to a Gaddi. The 1950 rates per goat and per sheep are listed on the same page.
One of the raja's officials received wool in place of revenue and made blankets for the raja.
Some forests were controlled by the raja's agents, and the villagers had access to them.
The ruler leased the Brahmni pastures to a contractor, who allotted them to shepherds in return for manure.
An attempt in 1874 to lease the high pastures was abandoned after opposition.
The Forest Department took over the grazing tax. A receipt is issued only to a shepherd who holds a permit.
Newell writes that the power of the Forest Department is paramount.
The Forest Department allots each shepherd a fixed pasture and charges Rs 15 per hundred sheep or goats.
The Forest Department grants no additional permits for more sheep and goats.
The fee is Rs 5 for a grazier without rights and Re 1 for a grazier with rights.
The villagers' grazing rights were granted by the early rulers of Chamba.
Passes are issued to check erosion. Grazing without a pass is punished by a fine or by forfeiture of the animal.
Some pastures were closed for soil conservation, and the villagers resent the Forest Department.
The table lists the sheep and goats that paid grazing fees from 1952-53 to 1961-62. The figures were read from the page image. A note describes 1959-60 as the year after a sheep disease.
Newell attributes a fall of a quarter in the flocks to the permit system. Shepherds buy and sell permits, and Newell calls them closed corporations.
Labourers prefer road work to work as fawals because wages on the roads are higher. The same page states that Shipki La was open to traders before the India-China dispute.
Eight persons work on roads and timber at about Rs 2 a day.
On average 24 persons, from every caste, work as unskilled labourers on roads.
Some members of every family work as unskilled labourers.
A shepherd reports that a jeep now runs on the track the shepherds have used for centuries.
The old trade route to Tibet over the Rohtang pass has been made jeepable from Manali to Keylong.
The surveyor writes that the new roads are likely to change the villagers' cycle of life.
The notes to maps 270 and 271 state that Kangra and Lahaul and Spiti had almost no metalled roads in 1947, and more by 1961.
Map 270 is a map of the metalled and unmetalled roads of 1947.
Map 271 is a map of the metalled and unmetalled roads of 1961.
Labourers building roads have migrated into Lahaul and Spiti.
The hill states were merged into Himachal Pradesh on 15 April 1948.
After the trade with Tibet stopped, wool and pasham were scarce.
The people of Chergaon used to buy wool at the Lavi fair, and now buy it from Dodra Kawar.
